title: The Map That Changed Its Mind
label: A Bizzing mystery
setting: the Seal Room, the Copying Room, the front desk

officeObject.name: a map-maker's compass (a pair of brass dividers)
officeObject.art: Ms Ito's brass dividers: two pointed legs, a hinge, a small knurled wheel; on the shelf, legs open, as if still measuring.

arc.beat: Raman postcard from Singapore: a rebus naming S. Pettigrew, Crane's lawyer, who "has ? ? ?" (doubts)
Silas Crane's letter claims the Library stands on Gull Wharf, which he owns
Mr Swale altered the map, paid by Crane (Swale returns as a suspect in Case 10)
Mr Pettigrew is nervous and honest (sets up his turn in Case 10)
Marlowe Finch suspected for the third time, and cleared
Ada tells the story of the Founding Charter and of Odile, her apprentice who left
The Blot Ledger reads UNDER THE CLOCK THAT NEVER STRIKES LIES EVERY…; Dev realises it is a sentence
Nell, for the first time, refuses to rate a hunch (her flaw begins to mend)
arc.note: continuity: in Case 7 she would not rate a hunch about a case; here, after slipping back to a ten on Marlowe, she refuses one about herself, her Inspector application. Quill's line marks the difference.

arc.beat: Seed (Odile), Chapter 1: the calling card is in a gap that was not there at seven, and the page smells of violets

Seed (the clock), deliberate: the caption says nothing ticks in the Seal Room; at Lantern Row Ada says every clock in the Library strikes, and Quill corrects her: only every clock they *heard*. Asha writes "Seal Room, no tick" in her margin. Nobody explains it.

card.text: Three hundred years ago, someone drew the harbour wall on the Library's Harbour Map. This week, someone drew it again, behind the Library, on Silas Crane's land. Four people hold a key to the map's locked room. All four say, "Not me." At five today, the new line goes into the Town Book. Unless you find who drew it.
card.clock: At five today, the new line goes into the Town Book.

cutscene.place: The agency, Wednesday morning, rain on the round window
cutscene.picture: Marlowe bursts in after the 39 stairs, gasping, holding a letter with a cracked wax seal.

lines.text: Breathe first. Then read it to us.
The Keeper says come now. The Registry's clerk comes at five, to copy the map into the Town Book.

cutscene.clock: The Registry's clerk comes at five.

cutscene.place: The Seal Room in the Scriptorium
cutscene.picture: cold stone, candle sconces, a long oak table, a dust cloth lifted from an enormous brown map. Ms Ito points with a gloved finger.
cutscene.caption: Everywhere else in the Scriptorium, clocks tick. In here, nothing does.

cutscene.place: The Seal Room in the Scriptorium
cutscene.picture: Close on the map: two harbour lines. One is old, dark and scraped faint. One is pale, new, and curves *behind* the Library's tiny painted dome.

cutscene.place: The Seal Room in the Scriptorium
cutscene.picture: Felix sneezes, so hard his head tips back towards the shadowy ceiling. Everyone jumps.

cast.name: Mr Rupert Swale
cast.title: Deputy Keeper of the Great Library
cast.look: Very tall and stooped, half-moon glasses on a chain, grey cardigan with leather elbows, a fountain pen clipped in the top pocket
cast.manner: Formal and polished; says "I assure you" exactly when he is least sure
cast.motive: Crane's thick envelope, and the promise of "Director of the Experience"
cast.secret: twenty years ago he was passed over for Keeper, and nobody has ever asked him to be first at anything (comes out at the reveal)

cast.name: Ms Kiyomi Ito
cast.title: map restorer (every Wednesday)
cast.look: White cotton gloves, a magnifying visor pushed up into short black hair, a canvas apron of tiny brushes
cast.manner: Brisk, exact and kind underneath; talks in numbered points
cast.motive: Crane offered her a well-paid post, and she is alone with the map every Wednesday
cast.secret: she nearly said yes, for her mother's roof: "accept" is under the first crossing-out

cast.name: Marlowe Finch
cast.title: assistant archivist
cast.look: Slight, ink on every finger, a tower of books up to the chin, a pencil behind each ear
cast.manner: Nervous and brilliant; over-explains; keeps count of how often he is suspected
cast.motive: (as it looks) a Seal Room key, ink on every finger, late on Tuesday, and Mr Swale's finger
cast.secret: he stayed late, unasked and unpaid, to rule forty pages so the new apprentices would not have to

cast.name: Mr Septimus Pettigrew
cast.title: Silas Crane's lawyer (Crane calls him "my assistant")
cast.look: Short and round, a brown suit one size too big, round spectacles he polishes when anxious
cast.manner: Apologises before every sentence; tells the truth when asked straight
cast.motive: he works for Crane and carried the envelope
cast.secret: in the spring he telephoned a library Crane had closed, to ask if it had been fair

cast.name: Quill

docs.title: Letter — Professor Orla Penhallow, Keeper
docs.author: Professor Orla Penhallow, Keeper
docs.where: carried up the 39 stairs by Marlowe Finch
docs.picture: a cream letter, the Library's wax seal (an open book) cracked in two.
docs.body:
To the Inkwell Detective Agency,
Please come to the Scriptorium at once.
Our Harbour Map is three hundred years old. This morning, it seems to have changed its mind.
The harbour wall on the map used to run in front of the Library. Now [[c:behind|it runs behind the Library]], as if we stood on Gull Wharf.
Mr Crane bought Gull Wharf in the summer. You can guess why that frightens me.
Ms Ito found the change [[c:itofound|at nine this morning]]. I checked the map myself [[c:monday|on Monday at ten, and all was well]].
The map lives in the Seal Room, and the Seal Room is always locked. Four people have been near it this week.
Every one of them tells me the map was never touched.
Bring your sharpest eyes.
O. Penhallow, Keeper

docs.title: RESTORER'S REPORT — The Harbour Map
docs.author: Ms Kiyomi Ito, map restorer
docs.where: clipped to the map's dust cloth
docs.picture: a typed report on squared paper, a photograph of the map paper-clipped to the corner.
docs.body:
Examined: Wednesday, 9:00 to 11:00 am.
1. I compared the map with my photograph from March.
2. One line is different: the harbour wall beside the Library. The old line has been scraped faint.
3. The new line is [[c:irongall|iron-gall ink]]. Iron-gall goes on pale. It turns darker as it dries, slowly, over many days. [[c:vinegar|Fresh, it smells sharp, like vinegar.]]
4. [[c:oldbrown|The old lines are dark brown]]. [[c:newgrey|The new line is pale grey]]. It [[c:notdried|had not dried]].
5. So the new line was drawn [[c:daytwo|in the last day or two]].
6. [[c:itonever|Restorers never use iron-gall. It bites into old paper.]] Everything I use can be taken off again.
7. Fresh iron-gall sits on the varnish for a few days. If we act quickly, I can lift it.
K. Ito, Map Restorer

docs.title: Log — Mr Abel Mensah, night porter
docs.author: Mr Abel Mensah, night porter
docs.where: on the porter's desk by the Scriptorium door
docs.picture: a ruled ledger with a brass key on a red tag lying across it; doodles of keys in the margin.
docs.body:
NIGHT PORTER'S KEY LOG — Scriptorium
[[c:keyholders|Seal Room keys: O. Penhallow (Keeper), R. Swale (Deputy), M. Finch (seal box only), K. Ito (Wednesdays)]].
After 5 pm, all keys are signed out at this desk.
Monday. No Seal Room key out. Rain.
Tuesday. [[c:mf510|5:10 pm, M.F., to return the seal box. Key back 5:15 pm.]]
Tuesday. [[c:rs840|8:40 pm, R.S., humidity reading. Key back 9:25 pm.]]
Tuesday. 9:30 pm, [[c:chips|Seal Room stair smells of vinegar. Someone's chips, I expect.]]
Tuesday. 11 pm, all doors checked. Quiet as a library. Ha!
Wednesday. Day staff took over at 7 am.
Margin note: R.S. took the small lamp. [[c:fortyfive|Forty-five minutes for one humidity reading!]] Very thorough, our Mr S.
A. Mensah, Night Porter

docs.title: Statement — Mr Rupert Swale, Deputy Keeper
docs.author: Mr Rupert Swale, Deputy Keeper
docs.where: typed and signed, handed to the Keeper
docs.picture: crisp Library notepaper, a fountain-pen signature with a flourish.
docs.body:
STATEMENT OF R. SWALE, DEPUTY KEEPER
I have served this Library for twenty-two years. I wish to help the Keeper in every way.
I examined the Harbour Map at eleven today, with the Keeper. [[c:matched|To my eye, the ink of the wall line matched the original perfectly.]] I believe that line has always been where it is now. Memory can play tricks.
I should add that [[c:notentered|I had not entered the Seal Room since spring]], until this morning. My duties keep me at the front desk.
If you want my advice, speak to young Finch. [[c:finchink|Finch was in the building late on Tuesday, with ink.]]
R. Swale

docs.title: Letter — Silas Crane
docs.author: Silas Crane
docs.where: in the Keeper's in-tray, stamped by the front desk
docs.picture: heavy cream paper, a gold embossed crane, a round rubber stamp in purple ink.
docs.body:
CRANE HOLDINGS — The Inkwell Experience
Dear Professor Penhallow,
Good news travels fast!
[[c:nowshows|As your own Harbour Map now shows]], the old harbour wall runs behind the Library. The Library therefore stands on Gull Wharf, which I own.
I am sure we can be friends about this. I will pay a fair price for the books. The building, of course, is already mine.
[[c:clerk|The Town Registry's clerk will call at five today to copy your map's new line into the Town Book.]]
Shall we say tea on Friday? I will bring the cake.
Warmest wishes,
Silas Crane
Purple stamp: [[c:recd830|RECEIVED — FRONT DESK — WEDNESDAY 8:30 AM]]

docs.title: Note — Tam Bellweather, for the Lamplighters
docs.author: Tam Bellweather, for the Lamplighters
docs.where: pushed under the agency door, smelling of cinnamon
docs.picture: a torn bakery bag, pencil, one greasy thumbprint.
docs.body:
tues nite — lamplighters report from tam
lit the scriptorium lamps 7 oclock. marlowe was in the copy room window [[c:ruling|ruling lines in a big book]] with a ruler. looked tired. waved at us
ivy says marlowe went out the side door [[c:mfleft|about half 7]] arms full of books as usual
then [[c:tallman|at twenty to nine a tall man with a stoop]] went up the seal room stair with a little lamp
[[c:bottle|he had a little bottle in his other hand]] like ink or medicine. we didnt see his face. he went very careful on the stairs like he didnt want to be heard
no sign of biscuit. sorry constable
— tam (and ivy and the others)

docs.title: Copy-book — the Scriptorium (rules); Marlowe Finch (the note below)
docs.author: the Scriptorium (rules); Marlowe Finch (the note below)
docs.where: open on the copyists' long desk, a calling card tucked into the gap
docs.picture: a huge ruled book, neat lamp-black lines, one empty space in rule 4 with a small white card lying in it.
docs.body:
THE SCRIPTORIUM COPY-BOOK — Rules for Copyists
1. [[c:lampblack|In this book, use lamp-black ink only. Never iron-gall.]]
2. Rule your lines before you begin.
3. Copy slowly. A hurried hand is a blotted hand.
4. A copyist checks [[c:gap|___ line]] against the original before the ink dries.
5. Sign and date your page.
Below, in a fresh hand: [[c:mfruled|Forty pages ruled for Thursday's apprentices. Lamp-black, as always. — M.F., Tuesday, 7 pm]]
In the gap in rule 4, a small white card with a perfect ink blot: [[c:card|"Eight now. Read them as one. — B."]]

talk.text: Marlowe, reading over the new detective's shoulder, goes pale.
That wasn't there at seven. I wrote my note right under rule 5. Rule 4 was whole. I read the rules every time; I can't help it.
Footnote: why does a copy-book smell of violets?
Nobody answers. A draught from nowhere lifts the corner of the page, holds it up for a moment, and lets it fall.

docs.title: Letter (draft) — Ms Kiyomi Ito
docs.author: Ms Kiyomi Ito
docs.where: on Ms Ito's worktable, under a glass paperweight
docs.picture: a handwritten draft with two crossings-out, a pencilled note in the corner.
docs.body:
Dear Mr Crane,
Thank you for your letter of last week. You offered me the post of "Chief Curator of the Inkwell Experience". You wrote that our maps would "look wonderful behind glass, with tickets".
It is a kind offer, and the pay is generous. [[c:decline|I must, however, decline.]]
A map belongs where anyone can lean over it and find their own street. [[c:nineyears|I have restored maps here for nine years, and nobody has ever paid to see one.]]
Please do not write again.
Yours sincerely,
Kiyomi Ito
Pencil, in the corner: [[c:posted|Draft. Fair copy posted Monday. — K.I.]]

docs.title: Visitors' book — the front desk; note by Mr Jide Oyelaran, desk clerk
docs.author: the front desk; note by Mr Jide Oyelaran, desk clerk
docs.where: on the front desk
docs.picture: a long ledger with columns, five different handwritings, a bell beside it.
docs.body:
GREAT LIBRARY — SCRIPTORIUM VISITORS' BOOK — Tuesday
Name · In · Out · To see · Purpose
Farah Quint · 10:05 am · 12:40 pm · Reading Room · Ship records
[[c:spin|S. Pettigrew · 3:50 pm · 4:05 pm · Mr Swale · To deliver a letter]]
Hollis and Bea Grant · 4:00 pm · 4:30 pm · Copying Room tour · Family visit
The front desk closes at 5 pm. [[c:novisitors|Visitors may not enter the Seal Room.]]
Clerk's note: [[c:envelope|Mr Pettigrew's envelope was thick and sealed. Mr Swale put it straight into his inside pocket.]] He did not open it at the desk.
J. Oyelaran, Desk Clerk

docs.title: Postcard — Dr Leela Raman
docs.author: Dr Leela Raman
docs.where: in the agency's post, addressed to Asha and Dev
docs.picture: front: orchids and a river at dusk; back: tiny drawings in a row (a tabby cat on a cushion; a musical stave with seven steps and a note on the top step; a seed, then a tall bean plant; three question marks).
docs.body:
Dear Asha and Dev,
Singapore is as hot as soup. I ate noodles at midnight under a tree full of lights.
I visited the old library by the river. Mr Crane closed it last year. The librarian told me something important.
One of Mr Crane's own lawyers rang her in the spring. He asked whether the closing had been fair. [[c:kindvoice|She said he had a kind voice and sounded worried.]]
His name is your puzzle, Dev:
[[c:rebus|S. + (our cat Pickle) + (the note seven steps up from doh) + (a seed, then a tall bean plant)]]
And what does he have? [[c:doubts|? ? ?]]
Asha, check my date before you trust me.
Love, Mum
Postmark: [[c:postmark|Singapore, Tuesday last week]]

talk.text: End of Chapter 1. Ms Ito lays the dust cloth back over the map, very gently, as if it might wake. Asha writes the time on her hand: 11:02. Six hours to the clerk.
Four keys. Four people. And every one of them says the map was never touched.
Then who drew on it? The map?

docs.title: Interview — Mr Rupert Swale, Q1
docs.author: Mr Rupert Swale
docs.where: Interviewed at the front desk. He stays standing, so the agency has to look up at him.
docs.body: At home, mostly, with a good book and a cup of cocoa. I left the front desk at five. I believe I came back briefly for my umbrella. One forgets these little things, at my age.

docs.title: Interview — Mr Rupert Swale, Q2
docs.author: Mr Rupert Swale
docs.where: Interviewed at the front desk. He stays standing, so the agency has to look up at him.
docs.body: I have already answered that in writing. [[c:notspring|Not since spring.]] I have no reason to go in. I am a front-desk man these days, I assure you.

docs.title: Interview — Mr Rupert Swale, Q3
docs.author: Mr Rupert Swale
docs.where: Interviewed at the front desk. He stays standing, so the agency has to look up at him.
docs.body: [[c:swaleink|Iron-gall, for signing the loan papers.]] It is a tradition, young lady. Three hundred years of tradition. Half the old families in Inkwell have a bottle in a drawer somewhere.

docs.title: Interview — Mr Rupert Swale, Q4
docs.author: Mr Rupert Swale
docs.where: Interviewed at the front desk. He stays standing, so the agency has to look up at him.
docs.body: That is a private matter, and I shall not discuss it. A man may receive a letter. Is there a rule against letters now?

docs.title: Interview — Mr Rupert Swale, Q5
docs.author: Mr Rupert Swale
docs.where: Interviewed at the front desk. He stays standing, so the agency has to look up at him.
docs.body: Changed? I am not convinced it was changed at all. But if it was, look for someone who was here late, with ink. Young Finch has ink on every finger.

docs.title: Interview — Ms Kiyomi Ito, Q1
docs.author: Ms Kiyomi Ito
docs.where: Interviewed in the Seal Room, gloves on, without looking up from the map.
docs.body: At nine, the moment I lifted the cloth. I always start at the harbour wall, because the Library sits right beside it. In my March photograph, the line runs in front. Today it runs behind.

docs.title: Interview — Ms Kiyomi Ito, Q2
docs.author: Ms Kiyomi Ito
docs.where: Interviewed in the Seal Room, gloves on, without looking up from the map.
docs.body: Never. Point one: it bites paper over the years. Point two: a restorer must be able to undo her work. Iron-gall cannot be undone once it has bitten. Point three: please stop asking.

docs.title: Interview — Ms Kiyomi Ito, Q3
docs.author: Ms Kiyomi Ito
docs.where: Interviewed in the Seal Room, gloves on, without looking up from the map.
docs.body:
He did. He offered me a job looking after maps behind glass. My answer is on my table, under the paperweight. Read it if you like.
*(A pause. She stops working.)* [[c:nearly|I nearly said yes. The pay would have mended my mother's roof.]] "Accept" is under the first crossing-out. I am not ashamed of the second one.

docs.title: Interview — Ms Kiyomi Ito, Q4
docs.author: Ms Kiyomi Ito
docs.where: Interviewed in the Seal Room, gloves on, without looking up from the map.
docs.body: The Keeper, every Monday. Marlowe, to fetch and return the seal box. Mr Swale holds a key, though he says he never needs it. [[c:stoop|He is so tall he has to stoop under the Seal Room door.]]

docs.title: Interview — Ms Kiyomi Ito, Q5
docs.author: Ms Kiyomi Ito
docs.where: Interviewed in the Seal Room, gloves on, without looking up from the map.
docs.body: Yes, if we are quick. Fresh iron-gall sits on top of the old varnish for a few days. I can lift it before it bites. After that, the harbour would stay wrong for ever.

docs.title: Interview — Ms Kiyomi Ito, Q6
docs.author: Ms Kiyomi Ito
docs.where: The Copying Room, at the start of Chapter 4.
docs.body:
Point one: scraping an old line faint, without making a hole, takes half an hour. At the least.
Point two: the new line, drawn steady, ten minutes more. Point three: by one small lamp, longer still.
[[c:fivemin|In five minutes, nobody could do it. Not even me.]] [[c:ittakes|In forty-five minutes, a careful person could.]]
*(She looks at the porter's log on the desk, and says nothing else.)*

talk.text: Marlowe had five minutes. Five to fifteen past five. *(She turns the hunch-o-meter face down.)* I'm taking the ten back.
I'm crossing you off my list. *(A pause.)* In pencil.

docs.title: Interview — Marlowe Finch, Q1
docs.author: Marlowe Finch
docs.where: Interviewed in the Copying Room, behind a wall of books. His fingers are inky. Nell's hunch-o-meter reads 8.
docs.body:
Ruling the copy-book. Lines, I mean! With a ruler! Thursday's apprentices need forty pages ready. [[c:mfblack|I used lamp-black, like the rules say. We're not allowed anything else in there.]]
Nobody asked me to. I remember my first Thursday, ruling till midnight. Please don't tell Mr Swale. He says I waste lamp oil.

docs.title: Interview — Marlowe Finch, Q2
docs.author: Marlowe Finch
docs.where: Interviewed in the Copying Room, behind a wall of books. His fingers are inky. Nell's hunch-o-meter reads 8.
docs.body: To put the seal box back on its shelf. Five minutes, maybe less. Mr Mensah wrote it down. [[c:mfcloth|The map was under its cloth. I didn't even lift it.]]

docs.title: Interview — Marlowe Finch, Q3
docs.author: Marlowe Finch
docs.where: Interviewed in the Copying Room, behind a wall of books. His fingers are inky. Nell's hunch-o-meter reads 8.
docs.body: [[c:onlyswale|Only Mr Swale. He signs the loan papers with it, at the front desk.]] He says it's tradition. It's banned in the Scriptorium, because it eats the paper.

docs.title: Interview — Marlowe Finch, Q4
docs.author: Marlowe Finch
docs.where: Interviewed in the Copying Room, behind a wall of books. His fingers are inky. Nell's hunch-o-meter reads 8.
docs.body: Mr Swale, actually. On the stairs, as I was leaving, at half past seven. [[c:umbrella|He said he'd come back for his umbrella. It wasn't raining.]]

docs.title: Interview — Marlowe Finch, Q5
docs.author: Marlowe Finch
docs.where: Interviewed in the Copying Room, behind a wall of books. His fingers are inky. Nell's hunch-o-meter reads 8.
docs.body: Because people keep returning them to me instead of the desk. Also, this is the third time I've been suspected this year. I've started keeping a list. You're on it.

docs.title: Interview — Mr Septimus Pettigrew, Q1
docs.author: Mr Septimus Pettigrew
docs.where: Interviewed on the Library steps. He would not come inside. "I don't think I'm welcome, and I'm not sure I should be."
docs.body: Sorry. Yes. Mr Crane asked me to carry an envelope to Mr Swale. So I did. I was in and out in fifteen minutes. The desk clerk will tell you.

docs.title: Interview — Mr Septimus Pettigrew, Q2
docs.author: Mr Septimus Pettigrew
docs.where: Interviewed on the Library steps. He would not come inside. "I don't think I'm welcome, and I'm not sure I should be."
docs.body: I don't know. It was sealed. It was heavy for a letter. [[c:thick|It felt as if there was money in it, and I have wondered about that ever since.]] I'm sorry. I should have asked.

docs.title: Interview — Mr Septimus Pettigrew, Q3
docs.author: Mr Septimus Pettigrew
docs.where: Interviewed on the Library steps. He would not come inside. "I don't think I'm welcome, and I'm not sure I should be."
docs.body: No. Visitors aren't allowed, and I've never asked. I've only seen the map in a photograph. [[c:redpencil|Mr Crane keeps it on his office wall, with a new line drawn on it in red pencil.]]

docs.title: Interview — Mr Septimus Pettigrew, Q4
docs.author: Mr Septimus Pettigrew
docs.where: Interviewed on the Library steps. He would not come inside. "I don't think I'm welcome, and I'm not sure I should be."
docs.body: Oh. Yes. In the spring. I wanted to know if what Mr Crane did there was fair. The librarian was very kind. She said it was not. I have had doubts ever since. Please don't tell him.

docs.title: Interview — Mr Septimus Pettigrew, Q5
docs.author: Mr Septimus Pettigrew
docs.where: Interviewed on the Library steps. He would not come inside. "I don't think I'm welcome, and I'm not sure I should be."
docs.body: I'm a lawyer. I'm supposed to say that I don't know. So: I don't know. But I know who I gave the envelope to. And I know whose wall that photograph hangs on.

deductions.statement: The new line had not dried, so it was drawn in the last day or two. The map was fine on Monday at ten. So it was changed between Monday at ten and Wednesday at nine.
deductions.why: It shrinks the whole week to one window. Only the key log entries inside that window matter.
deductions.also: [c:behind] "it runs behind the Library" is what the change *does*: it moves the Library onto Gull Wharf.
deductions.note: Vocab note: "dried" here means more than "stopped being wet". Iron-gall darkens as it dries over days, so a pale line is a young line.
deductions.label: The wall line is new, drawn between Monday morning and Wednesday morning.

deductions.statement: Mr Swale says he had not entered the Seal Room since spring. But the key log shows R.S. took the key at 8:40 on Tuesday, and R. Swale is the only R.S. with a key. The Lamplighters saw a tall man with a stoop on the Seal Room stair at twenty to nine.
deductions.why: Both cannot be true. This is the case's one checkable lie, told twice, and it sits inside the window from D1. (The porter's margin, [c:fortyfive] "Forty-five minutes for one humidity reading!", hints that the visit was not about humidity, and Ms Ito's answer in Chapter 4 says forty-five minutes is exactly how long the job takes.)
deductions.note: Sequence note: "twenty to nine" and "8:40" are the same time written two ways; the child links them.
deductions.label: Mr Swale was in the Seal Room on Tuesday night.
deductions.also: [c:notspring] "Not since spring." (the same lie, said aloud) · [c:ittakes] "In forty-five minutes, a careful person could." (Chapter 4)

deductions.statement: Mr Swale says the ink matched the original perfectly. But that is only 'to my eye'. The restorer's facts say the old lines are dark brown and the new line is pale grey. They cannot match.
deductions.why: Why would the deputy keeper insist on something anyone can see is false? Someone who wants the line to be "old" has a reason.
deductions.label: The ink did not match the original.

deductions.statement: The new line is iron-gall. Restorers never use it. The copy-book allows only lamp-black. Marlowe says only Mr Swale uses iron-gall, and Mr Swale says so himself.
deductions.why: It ties the ink on the map to one desk in the Library. (The "little bottle" the Lamplighters saw, [c:bottle], supports it. So does the porter's nose: [c:chips] "Seal Room stair smells of vinegar. Someone's chips, I expect." against [c:vinegar] "Fresh, it smells sharp, like vinegar." Half past nine, five minutes after R.S. gave the key back.)
deductions.label: The new line was drawn in iron-gall ink, and only Mr Swale uses iron-gall.

deductions.statement: Crane's letter says 'as your own Harbour Map now shows'. The front desk stamped it at 8:30. Ms Ito only found the change at nine. So someone told Crane before the Library knew. On Tuesday, Crane's envelope went into Mr Swale's inside pocket.
deductions.why: It gives the motive. The line was drawn for Crane, by someone Crane had paid. ("Good news travels fast!" is Crane almost boasting about it.) Mr Pettigrew adds the picture on Crane's wall: [c:redpencil] "Mr Crane keeps it on his office wall, with a new line drawn on it in red pencil." The line existed in red pencil before it existed in ink.
deductions.label: Mr Crane knew about the new line before anyone found it.

redHerrings.note: Suspicious because: ink on every finger; in the building late on Tuesday; holds a Seal Room key; Mr Swale points at him; Nell rates him an 8, then a 10. ruling means drawing straight lines with a ruler, not governing, and not drawing on maps. He left more than an hour before the 8:40 key. [c:fivemin] "In five minutes, nobody could do it. Not even me." (Chapter 4: his five-minute key could never have been long enough). His kindness is the clue: he tells the truth about seeing Mr Swale, though it makes him the only witness. Mr Swale's own pointing finger, [c:finchink] "Finch was in the building late on Tuesday, with ink.", tells us *he* knew who was in the building late.

Suspicious because: alone with the map every Wednesday; she found the change; Crane offered her a job. decline means politely say no; it does not mean "go down". She has no key after 5 pm on a Tuesday ([c:keyholders] "K. Ito (Wednesdays)"). Her secret makes her look worse first: [c:nearly] "I nearly said yes. The pay would have mended my mother's roof." Nearly is not yes. The posted refusal is dated Monday.

Suspicious because: works for Crane; carried the envelope; in the Library on Tuesday. Arc: the postcard ([c:rebus], [c:kindvoice], [c:doubts]) names him and shows his doubts began long before this case; [c:postmark] "Singapore, Tuesday last week" proves Dr Raman wrote it before the envelope was ever carried.

redHerrings.quill: The Blot has taken eight words away. Has the Blot ever *added* a line to anything?
redHerrings.note: Suspicious because: a calling card in the copy-book. The child may wonder if the Blot drew the line. The Blot hides words; it has never drawn on a document. This time it took one: [c:gap] "___ line" and left [c:card] "Eight now. Read them as one. — B." (the card is the Ledger beat, not a clue to the map).

arcMarks.note: The vanished word EVERY: the gap in rule 4 of the copy-book.
The Blot's calling card: the Ledger beat, not a clue to the map.

events.text: Ms Ito photographs the map; the wall runs in front of the Library
Mr Crane writes to Ms Ito offering a job; she declines and posts her reply
The Keeper checks the map; all is well
events.timeWords: "on Monday at ten, and all was well"

events.text: Mr Pettigrew delivers the thick envelope to Mr Swale
Marlowe returns the seal box to the Seal Room
events.timeWords: "5:10 pm, M.F., to return the seal box. Key back 5:15 pm."

events.text: Marlowe rules the copy-book in lamp-black
Marlowe leaves by the side door; meets Mr Swale "back for his umbrella"
Mr Swale takes the Seal Room key with a lamp and a little bottle; forty-five minutes, long enough to move a wall
The key comes back; the stair smells of vinegar
Crane's letter reaches the front desk
Ms Ito lifts the cloth and finds the change
The Keeper writes to the agency

shake.quill: Read the stamp again. Which came first, Crane's good news or our bad news?

evidenceRule.text: any 3 of these, of which D2 must be one

wrongSuspect.marlowe: Marlowe was *ruling* lines. Show me what that word means in Tam's note. Then tell me which ink the copy-book allows, and which ink is on the map. And ask Ms Ito what anyone can do in five minutes.
wrongSuspect.ito: Read her letter to Mr Crane again. What does *decline* mean, in that sentence? And who told us restorers never touch iron-gall?
wrongSuspect.pettigrew: Look at the visitors' book. When did he leave? And who is never allowed into the Seal Room?
wrongSuspect.blot: The Blot takes words away. This time someone *added* a line. Different hand, different habit.

accusation.weakEvidence: That shows someone was near the map. It does not show they drew on it. Find a place where a person says one thing and a document says another. Then find the ink.
accusation.note: Mr Rupert Swale, Deputy Keeper (paid by Silas Crane).

revealSetting: The Seal Room, Wednesday, a quarter to four. Rain on the tall windows. The map lies under lamplight. Everyone is there. Tully stands by the door with cocoa. Fifteen minutes to the clerk.

reveal.text: Mr Swale. You wrote that you hadn't entered the Seal Room since spring. You said it again today, out loud.
I did, and I assure you—
The key log says R.S. took the key at 8:40 on Tuesday. Tam saw a tall man with a stoop on these stairs at twenty to nine. Same time, written two ways.
And there's only one R.S. on the key list.
He kept it forty-five minutes. Exactly long enough.
And the new line is iron-gall. *(Sneezes.)* Only you use iron-gall in this building, Mr Swale.

And it is grey. The old line is brown. Nothing "matched perfectly". And at half past nine, Mr Mensah smelled vinegar on this stair. Fresh iron-gall smells of vinegar. It was in his log from the start. We all thought it was chips.
(The child pins three pieces of evidence on Swale's portrait. Quill reads them back.)
Four keys. Four people who said "not me". Three were telling the truth. And Mr Crane wrote "as your own map now shows" before anyone knew. Good news travels fast, Mr Swale. Who carried it?
(Swale sits down slowly. He takes off his half-moon glasses and folds them.)
Between you and I—
*Me.* Between you and *me*. Do go on.

*(a small, tired laugh)* Mr Crane said the Library would be sold anyway. One pale line would only make it sooner, and kinder. I could be Director of his Experience. Twenty years ago I asked to be Keeper. They chose Orla. They were right. Nobody has ever asked me to be first at anything.
(He takes the thick envelope from his inside pocket and lays it down, still sealed.)
I didn't open it. I couldn't. I drew the line, then sat here till the key was due back, looking at it. I told myself a line on a map hurts nobody.
A line on a map is a sentence, Mr Swale. It says who owns what. You wrote a false one.
*(quietly)* You could have told me you wanted more. I would have listened.
I know. That is the worst part. Orla, I am sorry.
(Above them, every clock in the Scriptorium strikes four. A damp clerk from the Town Registry puts his head round the door, a ledger under his arm.)
Thank you for coming. There is nothing to copy.

epilogue.text: The clerk goes. The rain eases. Nobody leaves the Seal Room quite yet.
*(to Marlowe)* I rated you a ten. I'm sorry.
You're off the list. *(A pause.)* Mostly.
*(to the Keeper)* And I nearly said yes to him, Orla. You should know that too.
Nearly is not yes, Kiyomi. *(She looks at Marlowe's inky fingers.)* And forty pages ruled for nobody's thanks is not nothing.
*(from the doorway, polishing his spectacles)* Sorry. I came to say I'm glad. I'll go now.
Stay for cocoa, Mr Pettigrew. Constable Tully always brings too much.

Ms Ito works until midnight with a brush as fine as an eyelash. The pale grey line lifts off the varnish like a breath off a window. Underneath, the old brown wall is faint but whole, running in front of the Library, where it has run for three hundred years.

Asha holds the brass dividers and walks them along the harbour, step by step, against the March photograph. "Every point matches," she says. "Every single one." Felix starts to say that *every* is the word missing from the copy-book. Then he sneezes, for the eleventh time.

Mr Swale gives the envelope to Constable Tully, unopened, and steps down as Deputy Keeper. He asks if he may help Ms Ito with the map's yearly clean. The Keeper thinks for a long moment, and says yes, "under supervision". He looks, for the first time all day, relieved.
Constable Tully finds Biscuit asleep in the map chest, in the wide flat drawer for the Southern Oceans, on top of a chart of the Antarctic. "Well," says Tully, "he's always liked it cool."
Ms Ito puts the dividers into the child's hands. "For the detective who checks every line," she says. "Keep them sharp."

epilogue.label: Office object
epilogue.text: the map-maker's compass goes on the shelf, legs open, as if it is still measuring.
Evening. Rain on the windows. Books in teetering towers. A cello leaning in the corner. Semicolon asleep on the lamp. Ada sits by the fire with a cup of tea she has already forgotten.
Well? You have the look of people with a puzzle in a pocket.
(Dev takes out his mother's postcard and lays it flat on the hearthrug.)
S, then Pickle. Pickle's our cat. Our pet. **PET.**
Then a note seven steps up from doh. Doh, re, mi, fa, so, la…
**TI.** Then a seed, and a tall bean. It **GREW**. S. Pet-ti-grew.
And three question marks. He has doubts. Footnote: *doubt* comes from an old word for wavering between two things. Which is exactly what he looked like on those steps.
Postmarked Tuesday last week. Mum wrote it before he ever carried that envelope. So his doubts are older than this case. He's been worried since the spring.
He told us the truth today, even though he was scared of it. *(She pauses.)* Someone with doubts might be someone who helps.
Keep his card.
(Dev nods, and opens the ribbon-tied Blot Ledger. He writes the new word in, slowly. Ink spreads into the page.)
Under. The. Clock. That. Never. Strikes. Lies. Every.
(He stops. He reads it again, without the gaps.)
It isn't a list. It's never been a list. It's a *sentence*. "Under the clock that never strikes lies every…"
Lies. Footnote: not *lies* as in fibs. *Lies* as in "is lying there". Like a cat lies on a rug.
Something is lying under a clock. Something the Blot wants us to find.
"Eight now. Read them as one." That's what the card meant.
(Across the room, Ada has gone very still. Her bow is in her hand, but she has not played a note.)
Every clock in the Great Library strikes. I know. Quill and I listened to all forty-one of them, one winter, forty years ago.
Forty-two, counting the porter's lodge.
That one strikes thirteen. It doesn't count.
It strikes. And forty-two is only the ones we *heard*, Ada.
That is what I said.
It is not quite what you said. *(He does not explain. He glances, just once, at the new detective.)*
(Asha opens her mouth, then shuts it again. In the margin of her timeline, very small, she writes: Seal Room, no tick. Then she underlines it, twice.)
(Ada puts the bow down. Mrs Achterberg comes in with fresh tea, looks at Ada's face, and sets the cup down without a proverb. Which, for Mrs Achterberg, is a kind of shout.)
Sit down, all of you. This is a long story, and I have told it to nobody.
(The fire settles. Even Semicolon opens one eye.)
Forty years ago, the Great Library nearly closed. The council said it cost too much. Every week there was another meeting, another vote, another word like "review". You will know that word by now.

People began to talk about the Founding Charter. The Library's first Keeper, Hannah Lark, wrote it in 1726. Three hundred years ago, near enough. It said the Library must be free, for everyone, for ever. If anyone could find it, no council and no buyer could ever close those doors. But Hannah Lark hid it, and nobody alive had seen it.
Quill and I were the best detectives in Inkwell. We thought so, anyway. And that autumn, I took an apprentice.

Her name was Odile. Odile Vane. She was eighteen. She arrived on my doorstep with a battered violin case and a notebook of puzzles she had made herself. She could find a pattern in a puddle. She saw the odd letter out before I had seen the word.
(Ada smiles, for the first time in the story.)

She wrote "forthwith" in everything. Reports, birthday cards, the shopping list. "Buy eggs forthwith." Winifred kept that one for years. And she signed every letter with a long dash before her initial, like a ribbon trailing off a parcel. I used to tease her that the dash was longer than the letter.
In the evenings I played the cello and she played the violin. We were terrible together. Wonderful, and terrible. Winifred used to shut the kitchen door.
*(quietly)* Two birds on one branch sing louder than they know.

All that winter, the three of us searched for the Charter. We opened panels. We lifted floorboards. We listened to forty-one clocks. Odile read Hannah Lark's account books, line by line, by candle. And she began to notice small things. A word underlined here. A word underlined there. She said, "Ada, the Keeper didn't hide it from us. She hid it *for* us. For whoever reads carefully enough."
I didn't believe her. I wanted fingerprints and footprints. I wanted proof you could hold in your hand. Underlined words seemed like a game to me.
Then, in the spring, the town saved the Library by itself. Children came to the Town Hall with pennies in jam jars. The council was so ashamed that it gave up. The doors stayed open.
And I closed the case. The Library was safe. I told myself the Charter did not matter any more.
Odile came to this room that night. She stood exactly where you are sitting. She said, "It matters, Ada. It matters for next time. There is always a next time."
And I said a thing I have been sorry for every day since. I said, "Puzzles are for children, Odile. Detectives deal in evidence."
(Nobody speaks. The rain ticks on the glass.)

In the morning her room was empty. Her violin was gone. On the step outside, she had left her magnifying glass, and a note. It said, "You taught me to read. One day I'll show you what it's for. — O." The long dash, even then.
I wrote to her for years. Every letter came back unopened. I don't know where she is. She would be fifty-eight now.
We were both wrong, Ada. I let you close it. I was tired, and I was glad of the rest.

No. *I* was proud. I could not bear a puzzle I could not solve, so I said it was not a puzzle at all. That is the worst thing a detective can do. *(She looks at the child.)* Write that in your notebook. Not because I said it. Because it is true.
(She picks up the cello. She plays a few slow bars. The tune seems to stop and wait, as if for an answer.)
This piece was written for two. For forty years I have only ever played half of it.
(She puts the bow down. Mrs Achterberg sets a hot cup in her hands and closes Ada's fingers round it.)
Old maps know the way home. So do old friends.
Winifred, that is not a proverb.
It is now.
Elementary; therefore!
(Laughter, a little wet. Ada looks at the child, and at the dividers poking from the child's bag.)
You checked every line of that map today. Not most of them. Every one. *(A pause.)* She would have liked you.
(On the way down the steps, Nell takes the unsent Inspector application out of the Comet's basket. Asha raises an eyebrow.)
Hunch-o-meter?
*(putting the form back, carefully)* I'm not rating this one. I'm going to wait for the evidence.
*(to the child, very quietly)* Mark the date. She has refused a hunch about a case before. Never one about herself.

epilogue.label: Arc beat
epilogue.text: the Blot Ledger, ribbon-tied, now reads **UNDER THE CLOCK THAT NEVER STRIKES LIES EVERY…** The last ink is still wet.

drill.title: The Log and the Statement
drill.instructions: The child reads a short gardener's statement and a shed key log, then taps the one sentence that cannot be true.

documents.title: Statement (Mr Pell)
documents.text: I love that shed. I painted it blue in May. I had not opened the shed since June. I keep my spade at home now.

documents.title: Shed key log
documents.text: 3 July, 6:15 pm, T. Pell, spade returned. 9 July, 8:00 am, A. Rao, mower out. 9 July, 11:00 am, A. Rao, mower back.

items.prompt: Tap the one sentence that cannot be true.
items.answer: I had not opened the shed since June.
options: I painted it blue in May.
I had not opened the shed since June.
I keep my spade at home now.
items.explain: The log shows T. Pell took the key on 3 July.

items.prompt: Mr Pell says: "I had not opened the shed since June." The new log says: "3 July, 6:15 pm, T. Pellow, spade returned." Can Mr Pell's sentence still be true?
options: No. The log proves it false.
No. Nobody opened the shed in July.
items.explain: Read every letter of a name. "T. Pellow" is a different person from "T. Pell". A log only catches a lie when the name really matches.

items.prompt: Back to the Library. The key log says: "5:10 pm, M.F., to return the seal box." The key list says: "M. Finch (seal box only)". Is M.F. on the key list?
items.explain: M. Finch has the initials M.F., and the reason matches too: "seal box only".

items.prompt: The key log says: "8:40 pm, R.S., humidity reading." Who on the key list has the initials R.S.?
items.explain: Only one name on the list starts with R and ends with S. When only one person fits, the initials point to them.

items.prompt: The visitors' book says: "S. Pettigrew · 3:50 pm · 4:05 pm · Mr Swale". Is S. Pettigrew on the Seal Room key list?
items.answer: No, and visitors may not enter
options: No, and visitors may not enter
items.explain: His name is not on the key list. The book also says: "Visitors may not enter the Seal Room."

items.prompt: Dr Raman's postcard is postmarked "Singapore, Tuesday last week". The visitors' book is for "Tuesday". Is it the same Tuesday?
items.answer: No, they are a week apart
options: Yes, the word is the same
No, they are a week apart
items.explain: Same word, different day. "Last week" moves the postmark back seven days. Like a name, a date must match exactly.

followUp.quill: Which word in his sentence makes it a promise about time?
And which words in the log prove it false?

drill.secondRound: A second round swaps in a red herring: a log line for "T. Pellow". The child must notice the name is not the same. (Round text added 5 Oct 2026, owner-approved; for sign-off with the case.)
drill.secondRoundQuill: Read every letter of a name, and every word of a date. A log only catches a lie when the name really matches.

backgrounds: The Seal Room (day): a vaulted stone room deep in the Scriptorium. Candle sconces, a long oak table, the Harbour Map under a linen dust cloth. Tall narrow windows, the light falling in slanted bars. Shelves of seal boxes, each with a wax-red tag. On the ceiling, half in shadow and never pointed at, a painted clock face with no hands. It must be present in this plate (the season's fair-play seed), but not lit, centred or emphasised. In opening panel 4, Felix's sneeze tips his head back towards it: the only eyeline in the case that goes near it. The words do the rest (the panel 2 caption "In here, nothing does", Asha's "I don't think it has one", and Quill's "only the ones we *heard*").
The Seal Room (lamplit, rain): for the reveal at a quarter to four; rain on the tall windows, lamplight pooled on the map, the rest of the room soft indigo.
The Copying Room: long desks, green-shaded lamps, rows of ink pots (black), the copy-book open, rulers, a window onto Lamplit Row where a lamplighter's pole is just visible.
The Copying Room (rain): for the board intro: rain running down the long windows, Tully dripping on the floorboards, green-shaded lamps lit at two in the afternoon.
The front desk: a carved oak counter, a brass bell, the visitors' book, a rack of loan papers, a small dark bottle in a pen tray (iron-gall; not labelled).

No. 9 Lantern Row (night): fire, rain on the windows, teetering books, the cello, Semicolon on the lamp, a forgotten teacup on the arm of the chair. Warm amber against teal shadows. Cosy, never sad-dark.
props: The Harbour Map: brown, old, a little painted dome for the Library; two harbour lines visible in close-up (one dark brown and scraped faint, one pale grey and crisp).
Ms Ito's brass dividers (the office object): two pointed legs, a hinge, a small knurled wheel.
The porter's key log, the thick sealed envelope, the white calling card with a perfect ink blot.

The Raman postcard: orchids and river on the front; on the back a row of tiny drawings (tabby cat on a cushion; a stave with seven steps and a note on the top step; a seed and a tall bean plant; three question marks drawn as shapes).
Ada's cello, Odile's magnifying glass (Ada keeps it on the mantelpiece, wrapped in a handkerchief; seen, not mentioned).
portraits: Mr Swale: calm, offended, nervous, guilty, relieved. His height must read clearly beside the others (he stoops under door frames in the cutscene panels).
Ms Ito: calm, offended, amused, relieved. Visor up for calm, down for working.
Mr Pettigrew: nervous, guilty, relieved. Shorter than Marlowe in any group panel, so the Lamplighters' "tall man" cannot be him.
Marlowe: reuse the model sheet; add ink on the fingers.
Ada: add a new expression for the story scene: remembering (eyes lowered, a half smile, the bow resting on her knee).
revealPanels: Asha's finger on the log beside Tam's bakery-bag note.
Ms Ito's gloved hand beside the pale line and the brown line.
The sealed envelope on the table, untouched.
The Keeper's face: not angry, sad.

seeds.brief: On the ceiling, half in shadow and never pointed at, a painted clock face with no hands. It must be present in this plate (the season's fair-play seed), but not lit, centred or emphasised.

art.sound: The Scriptorium's clocks striking three, then four, one after another down the corridors (never in the Seal Room); rain; paper rustle; a pen scratch as Dev writes EVERY into the Ledger; rain at Lantern Row; four slow cello notes under Ada's last line (recorded live, never synthesised; silent during read-aloud).
art.notes: No lettering in any painting. Every word on every document, card, book spine and sign is live text set by the app. The Seal Room day plate carries the season's fair-play seed: a painted clock face with no hands on the ceiling, half in shadow, never lit, centred or emphasised.

aside.text: Vanished word: EVERY (rule 4 of the Scriptorium copy-book)
Glossed words (once marked): iron-gall · ruling · decline · stoop · half 7 · lies (two meanings)
One suspect lies (Mr Swale): one checkable false fact, "not since spring", which he writes once and repeats aloud when asked. Everything else he says is dodging, not a fact a document can catch.
Crane's letter: the Town Registry's clerk will copy the new line into the Town Book at five today. Halfway, Crane has it moved to four.
A locked room. Four people hold Seal Room keys, and every one says the map was never touched by them. The one who went in on Tuesday (Marlowe) had five minutes, and nobody can move a wall in five.

End of Chapter 3, Nell's hunch-o-meter hits ten for Marlowe (ink on every finger, a key, late on Tuesday, Swale's finger, and the calling card turned up in his book). Broken at the start of Chapter 4 by Ms Ito: the job takes forty-five minutes, not five.
The porter's log, Chapter 1: "Seal Room stair smells of vinegar. Someone's chips, I expect." Fresh iron-gall smells of vinegar (Ms Ito's report). Paid off at the reveal.

Through the Copying Room window, the agency watches Mr Swale cross the courtyard in the rain. At the foot of the Seal Room stair he stops, takes the fountain pen from his top pocket, and looks at it for a long moment. Then he puts it back, and does not go up.
Ms Ito appears in the Copying Room doorway, peeling off her white gloves one finger at a time.
Before anybody writes a name down: has anyone asked me how long it takes to move a three-hundred-year-old wall?

aside.where: Chapter 4 — It opens with Ms Ito
aside.text: Ms Ito's Q6 (8.S2.Q6) opens at the start of Chapter 4; Nell takes the ten back.
Every clock in the Scriptorium strikes three, one after another down the corridors, like a staircase of bells. Then the building is quiet again.
Did you hear the Seal Room one?
No. *(A pause.)* I don't think it has one.

exercises.prompt: Ms Ito writes to Mr Crane: "It is a kind offer, and the pay is generous. I must, however, decline." What does "decline" mean here?
exercises.explain: "Decline" can mean "go down", like a hill or a price. Here it follows a kind offer, and "however" warns that a "no" is coming. So it means to say no, politely.

exercises.prompt: Ms Ito signs her report "K. Ito, Map Restorer". Restorer is "restore" + "-er". What is a restorer?
options: a person who mends old things
exercises.answer: a person who mends old things
exercises.explain: The ending "-er" often means "a person who does it": a painter paints, a baker bakes. To restore is to mend something old. So a restorer is a person who mends old things, like maps.

exercises.prompt: The porter writes that R.S. came for a reading. Which spelling is right? "8:40 pm, R.S., ___ reading."
exercises.explain: Humidity means how damp the air is. Say it in parts: hu-mid-i-ty. Each part has one consonant in the middle, never a double letter.

exercises.prompt: Tam saw "a tall man with a stoop" go up the Seal Room stair. What does "with a stoop" mean here?
options: his back and shoulders bent forward
exercises.answer: his back and shoulders bent forward
exercises.explain: "Stoop" has more than one meaning. It can be a step in front of a house. But a man cannot climb the stair "with" a step. Here it describes how he stands: bent forward, as tall people often do.

exercises.prompt: Put these in order, earliest first. Use the Keeper's letter and Ms Ito's report.
options: The Keeper checks the map, and all is well.
answer: The Keeper checks the map, and all is well.
exercises.explain: The Keeper checked "on Monday at ten, and all was well". Ms Ito found the change "at nine this morning", on Wednesday. Her report says she examined the map "9:00 to 11:00 am", so the report came last.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence sums up the Keeper's letter best?
options: Mr Crane has bought the Harbour Map from the Library.
A line on the old map has moved, and she needs help.
The Seal Room was left unlocked on Monday night.
exercises.answer: A line on the old map has moved, and she needs help.
exercises.explain: A good summary keeps the main point and drops the details. The letter is about one thing: the harbour wall "runs behind the Library" now, and she wants the agency to come.

exercises.prompt: Tam's note says Marlowe was "ruling lines in a big book" with a ruler. What does "ruling" mean here?
options: being in charge of a kingdom
exercises.explain: "Ruling" can mean being in charge, like a queen ruling a land. The words around it are clues: "lines", "a big book" and "with a ruler". Here it means drawing straight lines.

exercises.prompt: Ms Ito writes: "Iron-gall goes on pale. It turns darker as it dries, slowly, over many days." So what does a pale iron-gall line tell you?
options: It was drawn in pencil first.
It was drawn hundreds of years ago.
exercises.explain: The sentence after "iron-gall" explains it: the ink starts pale and darkens over days. So a pale line is a young line. That is why Ms Ito says it was drawn "in the last day or two".

exercises.prompt: Tam writes: "lit the scriptorium lamps 7 oclock." One word is missing an apostrophe. How should it be written?
exercises.explain: "O'clock" is short for "of the clock". The apostrophe stands where the letters "f the" were left out, right after the "o".

exercises.prompt: The porter writes: "Tuesday. 11 pm, all doors checked. Quiet as a library. Ha!" Why does he add "Ha!"?
options: He heard a loud bang at 11 pm.
He is in a library, so the simile is a joke.
He is cross about the rain.
exercises.answer: He is in a library, so the simile is a joke.
exercises.explain: "Quiet as a library" is a simile: it compares the night to a library. But he is sitting in one! He laughs at his own joke.

exercises.prompt: Ms Ito says: "Iron-gall cannot be undone once it has bitten." What does the prefix "un-" add to "done"?
exercises.explain: The prefix "un-" turns a word round: "tie" and "untie", "lock" and "unlock". To undo work is to reverse it. A restorer must be able to take her work off again.

exercises.prompt: Crane's letter is stamped "RECEIVED — FRONT DESK — WEDNESDAY 8:30 AM". Ms Ito found the change "at nine this morning". Which came first?
options: They happened at the same time
exercises.explain: Half past eight comes before nine. So Crane wrote "as your own Harbour Map now shows" before anyone in the Library knew the map had changed.

exercises.prompt: Mr Swale writes: "I had not entered the Seal Room since spring". The key log says: "8:40 pm, R.S., humidity reading. Key back 9:25 pm." The key list has only one R.S. What can you conclude?
options: The porter wrote the wrong day.
Someone borrowed his key in spring.
exercises.explain: Two documents say opposite things. The log shows R.S. took the Seal Room key on Tuesday. R. Swale is the only R.S. on the key list. So "since spring" is false.

exercises.prompt: Mr Swale writes: "To my eye, the ink of the wall line matched the original perfectly." Ms Ito writes: "The old lines are dark brown. The new line is pale grey." Which words show that Mr Swale is giving an opinion?
exercises.explain: "To my eye" means "this is how it looks to me". That is an opinion. Ms Ito gives colours that anyone can check: brown and grey. Brown and grey cannot match "perfectly", so the fact wins.

exercises.prompt: The porter writes in his margin: "Forty-five minutes for one humidity reading! Very thorough, our Mr S." What does he really mean?
options: The visit took far too long for one reading.
Mr S. is the best worker in the building.
The humidity in the room was very high.
exercises.answer: The visit took far too long for one reading.
exercises.explain: Sometimes a writer says the opposite of what he means. A reading takes a moment, so forty-five minutes is strange. "Very thorough" is a polite joke. It hints that the visit was about something else.

exercises.prompt: Mr Pettigrew says: "I don't know. It was sealed. It was heavy for a letter. It felt as if there was money in it, and I have wondered about that ever since." Which summary is fairest to him?
options: He counted the money inside the envelope.
He did not see inside, but he suspects money.
He knew it was only a letter.
exercises.answer: He did not see inside, but he suspects money.
exercises.explain: A fair summary keeps what he knows apart from what he guesses. He never saw inside the envelope. He only felt its weight. So he suspects money, and he says so honestly.

exercises.prompt: Dr Raman's postcard is postmarked "Singapore, Tuesday last week". She writes: "Asha, check my date before you trust me." Mr Pettigrew brought the envelope this Tuesday. When did the lawyer's doubts begin?
options: On the day he carried the envelope
exercises.explain: The postcard was posted a whole week before the envelope was delivered. The phone call to Singapore happened "in the spring", even earlier. So his doubts are older than this case.

exercises.prompt: Ms Ito writes: "Restorers never use iron-gall. It bites into old paper." Ink has no teeth. What does "bites into" mean here?
options: It eats into the paper and damages it.
It sticks to the paper like glue.
It makes a loud noise on paper.
exercises.answer: It eats into the paper and damages it.
exercises.explain: This is a metaphor. The ink is described as if it were an animal with teeth. Iron-gall slowly eats into old paper. That is why it is banned in the Scriptorium.

exercises.prompt: Ms Ito says: "I nearly said yes." Her posted letter says: "I must, however, decline." Did she accept Mr Crane's job?
options: No. She almost did, but she said no.
We cannot tell from her words.
exercises.answer: No. She almost did, but she said no.
exercises.explain: "Nearly" means almost, but not quite. She thought about saying yes. Then she posted a letter that says no. Nearly is not yes.

exercises.prompt: The key log says: "5:10 pm, M.F., to return the seal box. Key back 5:15 pm." Ms Ito says: "In five minutes, nobody could do it." Could Marlowe have changed the line?
options: Yes, he had the key that evening.
No. His key was out for five minutes, and the job takes far longer.
Yes, because he had ink on his fingers.
exercises.answer: No. His key was out for five minutes, and the job takes far longer.
exercises.explain: Count the time: 5:10 to 5:15 is five minutes. Ms Ito says scraping and redrawing takes much longer. So the time rules him out, whatever his fingers look like.

boardIntro.text: The Copying Room, two o'clock. Rain down the long windows. Constable Tully comes in dripping, with a note from the Town Hall.
Message from the Town Registry. Mr Crane asked them very nicely. The clerk's coming at four now, not five.

Then we haven't got time to be careful. Look at it. Ink on every finger. A Seal Room key. In the building late on Tuesday. Mr Swale saw him there. And the Blot's card turned up in *his* book, after he'd been at it.
Hunch-o-meter: nine. *(A pause.)* Ten. Sorry, Marlowe.
You're already on my list. You've been on it since March.
Show me where it says he drew a line, Nell. A ten is a number. It is not a reason.

extraMarks.note: The clock: the clerk copies the new line into the Town Book at five today (moved to four in Chapter 3).
